claims.text: Eastern Japan uses 50 Hz and western Japan 60 Hz.
Hertz measures cycles per second of alternating current. The illustrated 50/60 cycle comparison follows that definition.
Frequency conversion is necessary for power interchange between the two regions.
Common household supply is 100 volts; voltage is distinct from frequency. Not a claim about every Japanese outlet.
Appliance compatibility requires checking the manual or manufacturer, not assuming a matching plug is enough.

script.title: Japan's Electricity Has Two Rhythms | Japan Explained
script.description: Why eastern Japan uses 50 Hz, western Japan 60 Hz, and power interchange needs frequency conversion. Illustrative wave diagrams, not scale measurements. Common household voltage is distinct from frequency. #JapanExplained #Shorts

segments.text: Japan's power grid doesn't run to one rhythm. The east and west use different electrical frequencies.
Eastern Japan uses fifty hertz. Western Japan uses sixty. Hertz means cycles per second.
Think of alternating current as a repeating rhythm. In one second, the eastern supply completes fifty cycles, while the western supply completes sixty.
So sharing electricity across those regions takes frequency conversion. The power has to match the receiving side's rhythm.
That's different from voltage. Japan's common household supply is one hundred volts, but frequency still depends on the region.
A plug that fits doesn't settle compatibility. Check the appliance manual or ask its manufacturer.
The takeaway: electricity has both a level and a rhythm. In Japan, understanding both matters.
